Consider the following directed graph:

The number of different topological orderings of the vertices of the graph is _______.
figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 200" width="100%" style="max-width:420px;height:auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah-2016s1-cs11" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 Z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4" marker-end="url(#ah-2016s1-cs11)"><line x1="53" y1="90" x2="107" y2="58"/><line x1="135" y1="50" x2="175" y2="50"/><line x1="203" y1="58" x2="247" y2="92"/><line x1="53" y1="110" x2="107" y2="142"/><line x1="135" y1="150" x2="175" y2="150"/><line x1="203" y1="142" x2="247" y2="108"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><circle cx="40" cy="100" r="15"/><circle cx="120" cy="50" r="15"/><circle cx="190" cy="50" r="15"/><circle cx="260" cy="100" r="15"/><circle cx="120" cy="150" r="15"/><circle cx="190" cy="150" r="15"/></g><g font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="40" y="105">a</text><text x="120" y="55">b</text><text x="190" y="55">c</text><text x="260" y="105">f</text><text x="120" y="155">d</text><text x="190" y="155">e</text></g></svg>
explanation: The graph has edges a→b→c→f and a→d→e→f. Vertex a must come first and f must come last; the two internal chains b,c and d,e (each of length 2) can be interleaved in any order relative to each other, giving C(4,2) = 6 valid topological orderings.

Consider the two cascaded 2-to-1 multiplexers as shown in the figure.

The first MUX has input 0 tied to logic 0 and input 1 tied to R, with select line P; its output feeds input 1 of the second MUX, whose input 0 is tied to ¬R and whose select line is Q, producing output X.

The minimal sum of products form of the output X is
figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 220" width="100%" style="max-width:420px;height:auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah-2016s1-cs30" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 Z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"><rect x="110" y="60" width="110" height="70"/><rect x="290" y="60" width="110" height="70"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4" marker-end="url(#ah-2016s1-cs30)"><line x1="40" y1="75" x2="109" y2="75"/><line x1="40" y1="110" x2="109" y2="110"/><line x1="220" y1="95" x2="289" y2="95"/><line x1="150" y1="170" x2="150" y2="131"/><line x1="330" y1="170" x2="330" y2="131"/><line x1="255" y1="30" x2="255" y2="70"/><line x1="255" y1="70" x2="289" y2="70"/><line x1="400" y1="95" x2="415" y2="95"/></g><g font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="79">0</text><text x="20" y="114">R</text><text x="115" y="78">0</text><text x="115" y="113">1</text><text x="140" y="185">P</text><text x="240" y="20">R̄</text><text x="295" y="78">0</text><text x="295" y="113">1</text><text x="320" y="185">Q</text><text x="405" y="90">X</text><text x="150" y="105" text-anchor="middle">2-to-1</text><text x="330" y="105" text-anchor="middle">2-to-1</text></g></svg>
explanation: The first MUX outputs P'·0 + P·R = PR. The second MUX then outputs Q'·¬R + Q·(PR) = ¬Q¬R + PQR, matching option (D).

q:
Consider the transition diagram of a PDA given below with input alphabet Σ = {a,b} and stack alphabet Γ = {X,Z}. Z is the initial stack symbol. Let L denote the language accepted by the PDA.

The PDA has a start (accepting) state q0 with self-loops on a,X/XX and a,Z/XZ, an edge q0→q1 on b,X/ε, a self-loop on q1 on b,X/ε, and an edge q1→q2 (accepting) on ε,Z/Z.

Which one of the following is TRUE?
figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 500 220" width="100%" style="max-width:420px;height:auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah-2016s1-cs43" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 Z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"><circle cx="100" cy="140" r="18"/><circle cx="100" cy="140" r="23"/><circle cx="260" cy="140" r="18"/><circle cx="420" cy="140" r="18"/><circle cx="420" cy="140" r="23"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4" marker-end="url(#ah-2016s1-cs43)"><line x1="40" y1="140" x2="76" y2="140"/><path d="M85,124 C70,90 130,90 115,124"/><line x1="123" y1="140" x2="241" y2="140"/><path d="M245,124 C230,90 290,90 275,124"/><line x1="278" y1="140" x2="396" y2="140"/></g><g font-size="11" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="100" y="75">a,X/XX</text><text x="100" y="60">a,Z/XZ</text><text x="180" y="130">b,X/ε</text><text x="260" y="75">b,X/ε</text><text x="340" y="130">ε,Z/Z</text></g></svg>
options: L = {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0} and is not accepted by any finite automata
L = {aⁿ | n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0} and is not accepted by any deterministic PDA
L is not accepted by any Turing machine that halts on every input
L = {aⁿ | n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0} and is deterministic context-free
explanation: Since q0 is itself accepting, the PDA can accept any string of the form aⁿ by never leaving q0. Alternatively, from q0 it can push X's on a's, then pop them one-for-one with b's while moving to q1, and finally take the ε-move to the accepting state q2 exactly when the stack is back to Z, accepting aⁿbⁿ. This gives L = {aⁿ} ∪ {aⁿbⁿ}, and since the PDA is deterministic (no state has two applicable moves on the same input/stack-top), L is deterministic context-free, matching option (D).
